newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Profit-takers eat into coffee's latest surge.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Profit-takers eat into coffee's latest surge.

text.p: The price of coffee futures renewed their spectacular advance on Monday then profit takers in London and later New York moved in to blow the froth off the top of the latest rally.
Elsewhere in the commodity markets gold led a downturn in most of the precious metals.
As coffee producing nations led by Brazil began talks in London to see if they could help tame the world market, London futures for green robusta beans raced to new 15-month highs.
The benchmark July contract surged ahead $135 to $2,190 per tonne before easing slightly on profit taking.
In the U.S. the July price of the higher quality arabica bean type began firmer reaching $2.57 then fell sharply later by around 10 cents as investors sold to lock in their recent gains.
Low stocks, tight supply from Colombia and fears that Brazil, the biggest exporter, may have another frost have hooked speculators and triggered coffee's longest sustained rally for two decades.

The Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC), whose members account for 75 percent of world production, fear the rally may erode demand for coffee and turn people to cheaper substitutes such as tea or soft drinks.

Some of the 14 members wanted a suspension of export curbs but delegates said that a technical group of Brazil, Colombia, Ivory Coast, Indonesia, Uganda and El Salvador would propose retaining quotas, but with extra flexibility.
French, British and American consumers have been stung by new retail price rises in the past few days.
In the United States, Procter & Gamble unit Folgers Coffee Co. said it raised the price of a standard 13-ounce can of regular and decaffeinated coffee by 30 cents on Monday.
Precious metals prices fell again on Monday.
Gold, sentiment towards it shredded by news that the Germans may revalue their bullion reserves in a move linked to their budget deficit, sank with silver.
Gold slipped to a London fix at $341.25 an ounce, down $3.50 from Friday on fund selling.
Frail market confidence has been sternly tested since Wednesday night when rumours that Germany was considering revaluing its reserves first emerged.
"It has not really recovered from that," said one trader.
Dealers said the long term risk for the market was that gold would now be treated like any other asset which would be sold if it didn't earn its keep.
Silver fell four cents in sympathy with gold to around $4.67 per ounce.

Among industrial metals, London Metal Exchange copper probed last week's highs of $2,488 a tonne but, after failing on the upside, slid to end the London afternoon just $8 firmer at $2,474.50 in thin, technical trading.
Benchmark IPE North Sea Brent crude was kept above the $20 a barrel mark made last week by renewed buying by institutional funds and good fundamentals.
Wheat futures on the Chicago Board of Trade were down a couple of cents a bushel, on weekend rains in dry areas of the U.S. Great Plains.
